title: How to Safely Store Medicines at Home
excerpt: A few simple habits keep medicines effective and your family safe — here is how to store them properly at home.
imageAlt: Neatly organised home medicine storage shelf with labelled boxes and pill organisers

paragraphs: Most of us keep a small stock of medicines at home — pain relief, first aid basics, maybe a repeat prescription. Stored well, they stay effective and safe. Stored badly, they can lose strength, spoil, or end up in the wrong hands.

content.heading: Keep them cool, dry and dark
paragraphs: Heat, moisture and light are the three main things that degrade medicines. A locked drawer or high cupboard in a dry room beats the bathroom cabinet, where steam and temperature swings are constant. Keep medicines in their original packaging with the label intact so the instructions stay with the product.

content.heading: Keep them out of reach of children
paragraphs: Child-resistant caps slow children down — they do not stop them. Store all medicines high up or in a lockable box, including items you might not think of as dangerous, such as vitamins and herbal products.

content.heading: Check dates and dispose thoughtfully
paragraphs: Every so often, go through your stock and set aside anything expired, discoloured or crumbling. Do not flush medicines down the toilet or throw loose tablets in the bin — bring them to the pharmacy and the team will dispose of them safely for you.
list: Check expiry dates at least twice a year
Return expired or unwanted medicines to the pharmacy for safe disposal
Keep the original label with dosing instructions
Store any fridge items as the label directs

paragraphs: Unsure about a specific product? Bring it with you next time or send a photo on WhatsApp — the Medivyx team is happy to take a look and advise.

title: When Should You Speak to a Pharmacist?
excerpt: Pharmacists are one of the most accessible healthcare professionals. Here are the everyday moments when it pays to ask.
imageAlt: Pharmacist explaining medication instructions to a young mother

paragraphs: You do not need an appointment to speak to a pharmacist — you can simply walk in, call or send a WhatsApp message. For many everyday health questions, the pharmacist is the right first person to ask.

content.heading: Everyday moments worth a quick question
paragraphs: A surprising number of medicine problems can be prevented with a one-minute conversation.
list: Starting a new medicine and unsure how or when to take it
Taking several medicines and wondering if they can be combined
Mild symptoms such as a headache, cough, allergies or heartburn that are not settling
Choosing products for a baby or young child
Realising an old prescription is running out and wondering about refills

content.heading: When to see a doctor instead
paragraphs: Pharmacists handle everyday questions well, but some situations need medical review. If symptoms are severe, getting worse quickly, involve chest pain, difficulty breathing, high fever in a young infant or anything unusual after starting a new medicine, seek medical care promptly.
At Medivyx, asking is free. Message the team on WhatsApp or pass by the counter — no question about your medicine is too small.

title: Understanding Prescription Medicines
excerpt: Why some medicines need a prescription, what happens during dispensing, and how to make the most of it.
imageAlt: Close-up of a pharmacist holding a prescription document and a medicine bottle

paragraphs: Some medicines can be bought freely over the counter. Others — like most antibiotics and many long-term medicines — can only be dispensed against a valid prescription from a qualified prescriber. That rule exists for a good reason: these medicines need professional judgement about whether they are right for you.

content.heading: What happens when you hand in a prescription
paragraphs: The pharmacy team checks that the prescription is valid and appropriate, confirms the items and quantities, and then dispenses exactly what is written. This is also your moment to ask questions — how to take it, for how long, with or without food, and what to expect.

content.heading: Antibiotics are not for every illness
paragraphs: Antibiotics treat bacterial infections, not viruses like the common cold or most sore throats. Taking them when they are not needed makes them less effective for everyone over time. That is why Medivyx dispenses antibiotics only against a valid prescription.

content.heading: Make refills convenient
paragraphs: Running out of a regular medicine is stressful and avoidable. Submit your repeat prescription through the website before your supply runs low, and the team can prepare it ahead of your pickup.
list: Always take prescription medicines exactly as prescribed
Never share prescription medicines with others
Do not stop early because you feel better — finish the course if told to
Bring questions — the team would rather answer them than guess later

title: Essential Medicines for a Home First-Aid Kit
excerpt: A calm head plus a well-stocked kit handles most minor injuries at home. Here is a sensible starter list.
imageAlt: Flat lay of home first aid kit contents on a cream background

paragraphs: Minor cuts, grazes, headaches and fevers happen in every home. A thoughtfully stocked first-aid kit lets you deal with them calmly — without a late-night scramble to the shop.

content.heading: A sensible starter kit
paragraphs: Keep it simple and familiar. You do not need a huge stock — you need the right basics, stored in one place, in date, and out of reach of children.
list: Plasters and sterile gauze in assorted sizes
Antiseptic solution for cleaning wounds
Bandages, tape and a small pair of scissors
A digital thermometer
A basic pain and fever medicine such as paracetamol
Oral rehydration salts for stomach upsets
Hand sanitizer and disposable gloves

content.heading: Add what fits your family
paragraphs: Families with babies may add saline nasal drops and an infant-appropriate syrup. Someone monitoring blood pressure at home might keep their cuff with the kit. Tailor it — and refresh items after they are used.
Medivyx stocks a ready-made home first aid kit and every item on this list. Ask the team to help you build one for your household.

title: Medicine Safety Tips for Families
excerpt: From curious toddlers to shared prescriptions — practical habits that keep every generation safe with medicines at home.
imageAlt: Family organising a weekly pill organiser together at the kitchen table

paragraphs: When one household includes children, parents and grandparents, medicines in the home serve very different needs. These habits help keep everyone safe.

content.heading: One home, one storage rule
paragraphs: Wherever medicines live — a locked box or a high cupboard — apply the rule everywhere in the house. Handbags and bedside tables are where curious toddlers most often find medicines that are not theirs.

content.heading: Never share prescriptions
paragraphs: It can feel helpful to give a relative “the same thing the doctor gave me last time”, but prescriptions are personal. Age, conditions and other medicines change what is appropriate. Check with the pharmacy team instead.

content.heading: Help older family members stay organised
paragraphs: Weekly pill organisers make it much easier to see whether a dose has been taken. Offer to help set one up for an elderly relative, keep an up-to-date list of everything they take, and bring that list whenever they see a doctor or pharmacist.

content.heading: Teach children to ask, not self-serve
paragraphs: As children grow, teach them that medicine is not like sweets and that they should always ask an adult first. The habit sticks — and protects them when they are old enough to reach the cupboard.
list: Store all medicines in one agreed, secure place
Use a weekly organiser for regular medicines
Keep an updated list of medicines for each family member
Return expired medicines to the pharmacy for safe disposal
